tool.name: LandFacetDensity
tool.summary: For every land facet in a land facet raster, the proportion of the surrounding neighborhood that is composed of that facet, from 0 to 1. The result is one multi-band raster with a band per facet, computed in a single pass, rather than the one-raster-per-facet the original ArcMap Calculate Density Surface tool produced. The density surface is used twice in a Land Facet corridor analysis: areas of high density inside the Wildland Blocks become corridor termini, and density is one of the variables in the Mahalanobis cost surface, where its ideal value is 100 percent rather than its mean. Needs no Spatial Analyst. Part of the Land Facet Corridor Designer tool family.
tool.usage:
What this tool does. For each land facet in turn, it looks at the neighborhood around every cell and asks what fraction of that neighborhood is made up of that facet. If half the cells around a location belong to Land Facet X, the density of Land Facet X there is 0.5. Each facet gets its own band in a single output raster, so a 12-facet analysis produces one 12-band raster in one run instead of twelve separate rasters from twelve separate runs.
Why density matters. A cell can hold exactly one land facet, but a corridor needs more than isolated cells of the right type: it needs places where that facet is genuinely abundant. Density measures that abundance. Brost and Beier use it in two places. First, the highest-density regions inside each Wildland Block are converted into corridor termini, the start and end points of the least-cost corridor. Second, density becomes one of the variables in the Mahalanobis distance cost surface, alongside whichever continuous variables were used to define the facets in the first place. Elevation, insolation and steepness are the ones Beier and Brost recommend for topographic land facets from a 30 m DEM, and they are a sound default, but they are an illustration rather than a fixed list: any continuous topographic or soil variables may be used, chosen to suit the landscape and the question. The authors particularly encourage including soil variables such as depth or moisture wherever good soil data cover the whole planning area, since soil is at least as important as topography in determining what will grow where. In that role its characteristic or "ideal" value is 100 percent, not its mean, because the prototypical cell of a land facet is one surrounded entirely by its own facet. That is true even though the observed mean density is usually far below 1, which is exactly what the original method intended.
How the proportion is calculated (the denominator). The divisor is every neighborhood cell that lies inside the raster, whether or not that cell holds data. Two consequences follow. Cells beyond the edge of the raster are left out of both the count and the divisor, so a neighborhood that runs off the edge is renormalized to the part that remains and a cell at the very corner of the raster can still reach a density of 1. NoData cells inside the raster, by contrast, stay in the divisor and simply never match, so NoData dilutes the proportion. That is deliberate, and it reproduces the original ArcMap tool exactly. It also makes the result independent of how much of the rest of the raster happens to be populated, which is what allows a density surface computed here to be compared against one computed by the original tool, even though the original ran on a raster holding a single class and this one runs on a combined raster holding every facet. The alternative rule, offered under Advanced, divides by only those cells that hold data. That rule is not comparable across analyses: it would exclude the other classes on a single-class raster and include them on a combined one, giving different numbers for the same landscape. Use it only for a deliberate and documented reason.
How the values are stored. Density is a proportion between 0 and 1, but it is stored as an integer scaled by 10000, so a stored value of 6923 means a density of 0.6923. Divide the cell value by 10000 to recover the proportion. This is not a loss of precision that matters: density is a ratio of small whole numbers, so a 5-cell-radius circle of about 81 cells can only produce about 82 distinct values in the first place, far fewer than the scaled integer can represent. The reason for doing it is how much room the data takes up on disk or across the network. Band count multiplies everything, and 30 facets across a billion-cell grid is roughly 63 GB stored this way against 126 GB as 32-bit floating point. The scale factor is recorded in the output's metadata so the later tools convert automatically.
Which band is which. Raster band names do not survive being copied into a file geodatabase; the bands arrive named only Band_1, Band_2 and so on. The band-to-facet mapping is therefore written into the output's metadata, in the Supplemental Information field, as a small machine-readable record. The Mahalanobis tool reads that record to find the right band for each facet, together with the analysis identifier, the ordered list of the variables the clustering used, and the note that density's ideal value is 1. If the input raster was made by the Land Facet Clustering tool it carries a matching record of its own, and this tool will then label every band with its real category and cluster ("Valley, Cluster 2") and carry the variable order through. If the input carries no record, the tool falls back to the raster's distinct cell values with generic labels, which still works but leaves the later tools to ask you for the missing details.
How it looks when it is added to the map. Expect the output to look strange at first. ArcGIS treats it like any other multi-band raster and draws an RGB composite, feeding band 1 into the red channel, band 2 into green and band 3 into blue. What you see is therefore three unrelated facets' density surfaces mixed into one false-colour image, and any facet beyond the third is not drawn at all. Nothing is wrong with the data: the raster really does hold one band for every land facet, however many that is, and the run messages list them. To look at a single facet, open the Symbology pane, change the renderer from RGB to Stretch, and pick the band you want from the Band list. Every band carries its own statistics, so the stretch is meaningful the moment you select it. Remember that the stretched values run from 0 to 10000 rather than 0 to 1, for the reason given above.
Neighborhoods and units. All Focal-Statistics neighborhood shapes are available: Rectangle (width by height), Circle (radius), Annulus (inner and outer radius), Wedge (radius plus start and end angles, counter-clockwise from east), and Irregular or Weight from an ASCII kernel file (first line "ncols nrows", then the matrix; Irregular is 0 and 1, Weight holds weights). Sizes are given in Cells or in a ground unit (Meters, Kilometers, Feet, Miles). The original tool offered circular neighborhoods measured in cells, which remains the default. On a projected raster the neighborhood is a fixed number of cells; on a geographic raster, where ground cell size changes with latitude, a ground-unit neighborhood is sized geodesically per row, the same treatment the other neighborhood tools here use.
Performance and file size. The tool makes one neighborhood pass per facet and writes one band per facet, so both run time and the size of the file on disk grow with the number of facets. It reports the estimated file size before starting, warns past 30 facets, and stops past 200 on the assumption that the input is a continuous raster rather than a land facet raster. Bands are written one at a time and never all held in memory at once, so a large multi-band output is limited by disk rather than RAM. This tool honors no geoprocessing environments.
References. Land Facet Corridor Designer: Beier, P., and B. Brost. 2010, "Use of land facets to plan for climate change: conserving the arenas, not the actors," Conservation Biology 24:701-710 (https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1523-1739.2010.01422.x); Brost, B.M., and P. Beier. 2012, "Use of land facets to design linkages for climate change," Ecological Applications 22:87-103 (https://doi.org/10.1890/11-0213.1); Jenness, J., B. Brost, and P. Beier. 2013, "Land Facet Corridor Designer: Extension for ArcGIS," Jenness Enterprises (http://www.jennessent.com/arcgis/land_facets.htm). Corridor Designer tools: Majka, D., J. Jenness, and P. Beier. 2007, "CorridorDesigner: ArcGIS tools for designing and evaluating corridors" (http://corridordesign.org). Mahalanobis distance: Mahalanobis, P.C. 1936, "On the generalised distance in statistics," Proceedings of the National Institute of Sciences of India 2:49-55 (http://insa.nic.in/writereaddata/UpLoadedFiles/PINSA/Vol02_1936_1_Art05.pdf).

dialogReference.para: A single-band land facet raster, in which each cell holds the identifier of the land facet at that location and cells excluded from the analysis (outliers, cells above the confusion-index threshold, and anything outside the analysis area) are NoData. A raster produced by the Land Facet Clustering tool carries an analysis record that lets this tool label every band with its real category and cluster and carry the clustering variable order through to the Mahalanobis step. Any other categorical raster works too, but its bands will be labelled generically by cell value.

The output density raster: one band per land facet, in the order listed in the tool messages and recorded in the output's metadata. Values are integers scaled by 10000, so divide by 10000 to get the 0 to 1 proportion. A name is suggested from the input. A folder path typed without an extension is written as a GeoTIFF. Note that a large facet count produces a large file; the tool reports the estimate before it starts. When the result is added to the map it will be drawn as an RGB composite of the first three bands, which looks meaningless; switch the Symbology renderer to Stretch and choose a band to see one facet at a time (see "How it looks when it is added to the map" above).

Optionally restrict the output to particular land facets, one band each. Leave this empty to get a band for every facet in the raster, which is the normal choice. When the input carries an analysis record the list offers each facet by identifier and label; otherwise supply the facet cell values. Restricting the list is useful when only a few facets are being carried forward, or to keep the output small while testing a neighborhood size.

The neighborhood shape: Rectangle, Circle, Annulus, Wedge, or Irregular or Weight from a kernel file. Circle is the default and matches the original ArcMap tool, which offered circular neighborhoods only. The relevant size parameters below become active for the chosen shape.

The units for the neighborhood size: Cells, or a ground unit (Meters, Kilometers, Feet, Miles). The original tool measured its radius in cells, which is the default here. On a geographic raster a ground unit is sized geodesically per row. Not used for kernel-file neighborhoods, which are defined in cells.

The neighborhood radius (Circle and Wedge), in the chosen units. The neighborhood consists of every cell whose center lies within this distance of the focal cell's center. Brost and Beier used a 100 m radius for the density variable in their Mahalanobis cost surfaces.
The rectangle width, in the chosen units (Rectangle neighborhood).
The rectangle height, in the chosen units (Rectangle neighborhood).
The inner radius of the ring (Annulus neighborhood), in the chosen units. Cells inside this radius are excluded from the neighborhood.
The outer radius of the ring (Annulus neighborhood), in the chosen units. Must be greater than the inner radius.
The wedge's starting angle in degrees, measured counter-clockwise from east (Wedge neighborhood). The wedge spans counter-clockwise from the start angle to the end angle.
The wedge's ending angle in degrees, measured counter-clockwise from east (Wedge neighborhood).

An ASCII kernel file for the Irregular or Weight neighborhood: the first line is "ncols nrows", followed by the matrix. Irregular files use 0 (excluded) and 1 (included); Weight files hold weights, where 0 excludes a cell. The kernel is centered on each cell and is defined in cells.

What the facet count is divided by. The default, Every neighborhood cell inside the raster, reproduces the original ArcMap tool: NoData cells inside the raster stay in the divisor and dilute the proportion, while cells beyond the raster edge are excluded from both sides so edge neighborhoods are renormalized. This is the rule to use, and it is the only one whose values are comparable between analyses and against results from the original tool. The alternative, Only neighborhood cells that hold data, ignores NoData entirely; because that makes the proportion depend on how much of the raster happens to be populated, the same landscape yields different values on a single-facet raster than on a combined one. The tool warns when it is selected.

scriptExample.title: Land Facet Density example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: A density raster over a 3-cell circle for every facet, then a 100 m circle matching the published method, then a run restricted to two facets. neighborhood: "Rectangle", "Circle", "Annulus", "Wedge", "Irregular", "Weight". nbr_units: "Cells", "Meters", "Kilometers", "Feet", "Miles". Unused neighborhood arguments may be left as-is; only the ones for the chosen shape are read. Remember that the output holds integers scaled by 10000, so divide by 10000 to get the 0 to 1 proportion.
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
# One band per land facet, over a 3-cell-radius circle arcpy.jenness.LandFacetDensity( "landfacets.tif", "landfacets_Density.tif", None, "Circle", "Cells", 3)
# A 100 m radius circle, the neighborhood used by Brost and Beier arcpy.jenness.LandFacetDensity( "landfacets.tif", "landfacets_Density_100m.tif", None, "Circle", "Meters", 100)
# Only facets 3 and 7, to keep the output small while testing arcpy.jenness.LandFacetDensity( "landfacets.tif", "landfacets_Density_subset.tif", "3;7", "Circle", "Cells", 3)
